title: How to Find a Contingency Fee Lawyer: Referrals and Red Flags
description: A guide (not a directory) to finding a contingency fee lawyer: state bar referral services by state, screening questions, agreement checks and red flags.
h1: How to find a contingency fee lawyer
summary: The most reliable starting point is your state bar's lawyer referral service, which screens participating lawyers and in some states caps the cost of the first consultation. Before you sign, get the contingency agreement in writing, check the percentage at each stage, how costs are handled and whether a statute caps the fee, and confirm the lawyer's license with the state bar. Be cautious about anyone who contacts you uninvited after an accident.
body:
What this guide is, and is not

This page is not a directory or a matching tool. We do not list, rank or recommend individual lawyers. It explains where to look, how to screen the lawyers you find and what to check before you sign. For how the fee itself works, see contingency fees explained.

Contingency fees are common in personal injury, medical malpractice, some employment and consumer claims, and claims for certain benefits. They are not available for criminal defense, or in divorce matters where the fee would depend on securing the divorce or on the amount of support or property awarded[1].

Where to look

  1. Your state bar's lawyer referral service. Referral services match you with a participating lawyer in the right practice area. Some charge nothing for the referral itself, as in Kansas[2], and some cap the first consultation, for example at $25 or less for 30 minutes in Illinois[3] or $50 in North Carolina[4]. Contingency lawyers often waive even that fee for a case they want to evaluate.
  2. Personal recommendations from people who had a similar case, or from a lawyer you already know in another field.
  3. Legal aid, if your income is low. Legal aid programs usually send injury-type cases to private lawyers first, but they may help if two private lawyers have turned the case down[5]. See the legal aid guide.
  4. Lawyer advertising and online listings are fine as a starting list, but screen those lawyers the same way. Ask who will actually handle your case, because some firms that advertise widely refer cases to other firms.

If one lawyer refers you to another and they split the fee, ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) requires your written agreement to the arrangement, including each lawyer's share, and the total fee must still be reasonable[1].

In those states, check the state bar's website for a lawyer search, ask a county or city bar association, or contact the legal aid program listed in our legal aid directory.

Screening questions for the first call

  • How many cases like mine have you handled, and how recently?
  • Who will work on my case day to day, and who will I talk to?
  • What percentage do you charge at each stage, and what triggers a higher percentage?
  • Are case costs deducted before or after your fee? Do I owe costs if we lose?
  • Is there a statute or court rule that caps the fee in this type of case?
  • How will medical liens or insurance reimbursement claims be handled?
  • What is the deadline for filing my claim, and when would you file?
  • Will any other firm be involved or share the fee?
  • How and how often will you update me?

Talking to two or three lawyers before signing is normal, and contingency consultations are often free.

Check the agreement before you sign

Under ABA Model Rule 1.5(c), a contingency agreement must be in writing and signed by you, and must state the percentage for settlement, trial or appeal, the expenses to be deducted, whether they are deducted before or after the fee, and any expenses you owe regardless of outcome. At the end, the lawyer must give you a written statement showing how the recovery was divided[1].

Some states add more. In Florida, the lawyer must give you a signed Statement of Client's Rights before you sign, and the contract must let you cancel within 3 business days[6]. Some fees are capped by law, for example 20% or 25% under the Federal Tort Claims Act[7] and 25% or 33% in California medical malpractice cases[8]. The full list we verified is in contingency fees explained, and you can test the numbers with the contingency fee calculator.

Red flags

  • Uninvited contact after an accident. State ethics rules restrict lawyers from soliciting clients through live, in-person or real-time contact when the motive is a fee; Massachusetts' rule, for example, bars it except with other lawyers, people who have a family, close personal or prior professional relationship with the lawyer, and certain business or organizational contacts, and it bars any solicitation involving coercion, duress or harassment[9]. After an airline crash, federal law bars attorneys from unsolicited communications with victims or relatives about a lawsuit before the 45th day after the accident[10].
  • Pressure to sign on the spot, at the hospital, at home or by text, before you have read the agreement.
  • Promises of a specific settlement amount or a guaranteed win.
  • Vague answers about costs, or an agreement that does not say whether costs come out before or after the fee.
  • An upfront payment demanded for what is described as a contingency case, without a clear explanation of what it is for.
  • A percentage above a legal cap that applies to your type of case.
  • A "case runner", tow operator or medical office steering you to a particular lawyer.

Verify the lawyer

Every state bar or licensing authority has an online search showing whether a lawyer is licensed and in good standing, and many show public discipline. Check the name exactly as it appears on the agreement. Your state guide links to the state bar and its fee dispute program where we found one.

If no lawyer will take the case

Contingency lawyers decline cases when they judge that the likely recovery will not cover the work and costs, when liability is unclear, or when a deadline has passed. A refusal is not a ruling on your claim. Options:

  • Ask each lawyer why, and whether another type of lawyer would be a better fit.
  • Get a second or third opinion through a referral service.
  • Ask about hourly or flat-fee help with a limited part of the claim.
  • For smaller amounts, consider small claims court.
  • If you are low-income and two private lawyers have said no, ask legal aid again[5].

faq.q: Do contingency lawyers charge for the first consultation?
faq.a: Many do not, because they are paid only if they take the case and recover money. If you go through a bar referral service, the service may charge a small referral or consultation fee, which varies by state.

faq.q: Why would a lawyer turn down my case?
faq.a: Common reasons are that the expected recovery is too small to cover the work and costs, liability is unclear, the deadline is close or past, or the case is outside the lawyer's practice area. Ask for the reason and for a referral.

faq.q: Is it legal for a lawyer to contact me after an accident?
faq.a: Lawyers may advertise, but state ethics rules restrict live, in-person or real-time solicitation for a fee, and federal law bars unsolicited attorney contact with airline crash victims and their relatives for 45 days. You can report improper solicitation to your state bar.

faq.q: Can I change lawyers in the middle of a contingency case?
faq.a: Generally you can discharge your lawyer, but the first lawyer may be entitled to be paid for work already done, usually out of the eventual recovery. Read the termination clause and ask the new lawyer how the fee would be shared.

faq.q: Does a bar referral service guarantee the lawyer is good?
faq.a: No. Referral services typically check that participating lawyers are licensed and practice in the relevant area, but they do not guarantee results. Screen the lawyer yourself using the questions on this page.
